analysis.one_liner: Bans a high-dose, abuse-prone opioid painkiller unless it is reformulated to prevent abuse.
analysis.headline: The bill to pull Zohydro ER off the market never got a House vote; it died in the Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Zohydro ER is a time-released hydrocodone painkiller with no abuse-deterrent design. FDA approved it even though its own expert advisory committee voted 11 to 2 against approval, and attorneys general from 28 states asked the agency to reconsider. This bill would withdraw the drug's approval within 45 days and block approval of any version not formulated to resist abuse. It never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of opioid addiction and overdose, their families, and communities hit by prescription opioid deaths. The bill's own findings note CDC data showing prescription-opioid deaths more than quadrupled from 4,030 in 1999 to 16,651 in 2010, and that Zohydro's time-release can be easily defeated to produce a heroin-like effect. Because the drug offers no abuse deterrent and alternative pain medicines were widely available, the public health burden outweighed its benefits according to the bill's findings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of opioid addiction

how_it_helps.text: Within 45 days of enactment, the drug's FDA approval would be legally deemed withdrawn, ending its sale and distribution.
The FDA would be barred from approving any pure hydrocodone extended-release capsule unless it is formulated to prevent abuse, closing the door on a reapproval of the same product.

The bill responds to a specific documented hazard: the advisory committee found available dosages carried up to 10 times more hydrocodone than any hydrocodone painkiller then on the market, and the time-release effect is easily negated by abusers.

analysis.who_pays: Zogenix, the company that made Zohydro ER, would lose its approved product and the revenue tied to it. Some patients with severe chronic pain could face a slightly narrower set of opioid options, though the bill's findings state that alternative pain medicines and methods were widely available.

drawbacks.text: Some patients with severe chronic pain could lose access to a long-acting hydrocodone option, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even though the bill argues alternatives are widely available.

The bill overrides the FDA's scientific approval process by statute. Congress generally delegates drug safety judgments to the agency's experts, and this bill would have Congress itself deem an approved drug unapproved — a precedent critics of legislative micromanagement of drug regulation would flag, even though in this case FDA's own advisory committee had voted 11 to 2 against approval.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit clearly outweighed the cost. FDA's own expert advisory committee voted 11 to 2 against approving Zohydro ER, the drug lacked any abuse-deterrent formulation, its time-release could be defeated for a heroin-like high, and alternative pain medicines were widely available. The main costs fall on one manufacturer and, marginally, on a small set of patients, while the risk removed was contributing to an epidemic that had already quadrupled prescription-opioid deaths.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the bill on March 13, 2014, with 12 original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken: no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action appears in the record before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Zogenix, the maker of Zohydro ER, is better off because the bill died: the drug stayed on the market with no abuse-deterrent requirement. Members of Congress who preferred not to take a recorded vote on an opioid safety measure were also spared a politically charged vote.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw Zohydro ER's approval and bar approval of any non-abuse-deterrent version.

for.name: 18 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in the House.

for.name: Attorneys general of 28 states
for.what_they_did: Asked the FDA to reconsider its approval of Zohydro ER, as cited in the bill's findings.

for.name: FDA Anesthetic and Analgesic Drug Products Advisory Committee
for.what_they_did: Voted 11 to 2 against approval of Zohydro ER, citing the high possibility for addiction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over drug safety
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the health subcommittee, and never took it up before the Congress ended.

against.name: FDA (Office of the Commissioner)
against.what_they_did: Approved Zohydro ER without an abuse-deterrent formulation despite its advisory committee's 11-to-2 vote against approval, the action the bill sought to reverse.

against.name: Zogenix
against.what_they_did: Marketed and sold the approved drug that the bill would have banned; the bill's death left its approval intact.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan in the House — the 18 cosponsors split 14 Democrats and 4 Republicans, including Rep. Harold Rogers of Kentucky — and the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have withdrawn approval of its sole approved high-dose opioid within 45 days and barred reapproval without abuse-deterrent design. Its interest in keeping the drug on the market ran directly against the public-safety findings in the bill, which cite an 11-to-2 advisory committee vote against approval and easily defeated time-release.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical manufacturers of abuse-deterrent opioid formulations
industries.note: By requiring abuse-deterrent formulation for pure hydrocodone extended-release products, the bill would push the market toward reformulated versions, an area where manufacturers holding such patents stand to gain. Alternative pain medicine makers also benefit from keeping a cheap, high-abuse competitor off the market.
